author: BookingModel Editorial
title: How NoodleCo achieved 3.4x ROAS with 12 micro-creator videos on TikTok Shop
summary: NoodleCo partnered with 12 food and lifestyle micro-creators for a 30-day TikTok Shop campaign. The result was 3.4x ROAS and 2.1M organic views — beating their paid media benchmarks by 60 percent.
body:
NoodleCo sells instant ramen kits direct to consumers in the US. Before this campaign their paid social was carried entirely by studio-produced product shots, and their blended ROAS on TikTok had been stuck around 2.1x for two quarters.

The team wanted to test whether creator-made content could move that number without increasing spend. They ran a single 30-day campaign on BookingModel with a fixed budget and no additional media buying.

## The setup

Rather than booking a handful of large accounts, NoodleCo booked twelve micro-creators in the food and lifestyle niches, each between 15,000 and 80,000 followers. The brief asked for one thing only: show the product being cooked and eaten in a real kitchen, in under 30 seconds, with the price on screen.

- 12 creators, all US-based, all with TikTok Shop already enabled
- 2 videos per creator, delivered inside 14 days
- Full commercial usage rights, so every asset could also run as a Spark Ad
- One round of revisions, used on only 3 of the 24 videos

## What ran

All 24 videos went live organically first. The seven that cleared a 4 percent engagement rate in the first 48 hours were then promoted as Spark Ads using the creator's own handle, which kept the native look intact.

The remaining videos stayed organic. That split mattered: it meant paid budget only ever went behind creative that had already proven it could hold attention without support.

## The result

Over the 30-day window the campaign produced 3.4x ROAS against blended spend, and 2.1M organic views on top of the paid delivery. Cost per acquisition fell 38 percent compared with the previous quarter's studio creative.

- 3.4x ROAS, against a 2.1x paid media benchmark
- 2.1M organic views across 24 videos
- 38 percent lower CPA than the previous quarter
- 24 reusable assets, licensed in perpetuity

## What we would repeat

The single biggest lever was letting creators cook in their own kitchens instead of shipping a shot list. The videos that performed worst were the three that followed the brief most literally.

NoodleCo has since moved to a rolling monthly booking of eight creators, using the top performers from each month as the paid creative for the next.

author: BookingModel Product
title: BookingModel launches AI brief writer for faster campaign setup
summary: New AI brief writer helps brands generate creator briefs in under 3 minutes. Early beta users reported 40 percent faster campaign launch times.
body:
Writing a good creator brief is the part of campaign setup that most often stalls a launch. Brands know their product, but translating that into instructions a creator can act on takes a specific kind of writing — and doing it twelve times for twelve creators takes an afternoon.

The AI brief writer, now available to every brand account, drafts that document from a short description of the product and the goal.

## How it works

You answer four questions: what the product is, who it is for, what the video should make someone do, and which platform it runs on. The brief writer returns a complete draft covering hook direction, must-say messaging, shot suggestions, do-not-say constraints and delivery specs.

- Available from the campaign builder in your dashboard
- Drafts in under 3 minutes, editable line by line before it is sent
- Platform-aware: TikTok, Reels, Shorts and Meta feed each get different pacing notes
- Every generated brief stays editable; nothing is sent to creators without your approval

## What the beta showed

Across 60 brands in the closed beta, campaigns using a generated brief went live 40 percent faster than campaigns written from scratch. Revision rates dropped too — briefs that specified the hook explicitly cut round-two revisions roughly in half.

The pattern was consistent: the value was less in the writing and more in the checklist. Brands that had never thought to state a do-not-say constraint started stating one.

## What is next

We are working on brief templates per vertical, and on carrying the top-performing brief from one campaign into the next automatically. Both are targeted for the next release.

author: BookingModel Editorial
title: PowerFit Pro: 20% lower CPA after switching to UGC creatives
summary: PowerFit Pro replaced agency-produced ads with BookingModel UGC across Meta and TikTok. CPA dropped 20 percent in the first 30 days.
body:
PowerFit Pro is a supplement brand that had spent two years running polished agency creative on Meta. The work looked good and performed acceptably, but cost per acquisition had been climbing steadily as the same three ad concepts fatigued.

## The problem with one good ad

The brand's best-performing asset had been running for eleven months. Frequency was above 4.0 in their core audience, and every attempt to refresh it through the agency took six weeks and cost more than the media it replaced.

What they needed was not a better ad. It was more ads, faster, at a cost that made testing cheap.

## The switch

PowerFit Pro booked eight creators for unboxing and first-impression content, then ran every asset as a separate ad set with no creative favouritism. Nothing was pre-judged internally.

- 8 creators, 16 videos, delivered in 12 days
- Every video tested independently on Meta and TikTok
- Budget held flat against the previous month
- Winners scaled at day 7, losers cut at day 4

## The result

CPA fell 20 percent within the first 30 days, and click cost settled at $0.42 against a $0.61 baseline. Two of the sixteen videos accounted for most of the gain — which is the point. The other fourteen cost very little to find out about.

## The lesson

UGC did not beat the agency creative because it was better made. It beat it because sixteen cheap attempts find a winner more reliably than one expensive attempt, and because a creator can reshoot in three days when the agency needs six weeks.

author: BookingModel Editorial
title: Meet Jess M. — Austin creator earning $4,200/mo from UGC alone
summary: Jess started creating UGC content 18 months ago. Today she earns a full-time income from brand partnerships booked through BookingModel.
body:
Jess M. is a UGC creator based in Austin, Texas. She has fewer than 9,000 followers and has never had a video go viral. She also earns more from content than she did from the marketing job she left eighteen months ago.

## Not an influencer

The distinction matters. Jess is not paid for her audience — most of her work never appears on her own account at all. Brands book her to produce content they run themselves, as ads.

That changes what she optimises for. Follower count is irrelevant; delivery reliability, a usable home studio corner and the ability to take direction are what get her rebooked.

## The setup

- A window-lit corner of a spare room, one $90 light for evenings
- iPhone on a tripod, a $40 lavalier microphone
- Roughly 6 hours a week filming, 4 hours editing
- 12 to 18 videos delivered per month across 4 to 6 brands

## The numbers

Jess averages $4,200 a month. Her per-video rate started at $65 and now sits between $180 and $250 depending on scope and usage terms. About 70 percent of her bookings are repeat clients.

## Her advice

"Deliver early. That is the whole thing. Brands are not comparing your lighting to a studio, they are comparing you to the last creator who went quiet for a week. Being the person who sends the files on Tuesday when you said Wednesday is worth more than any camera upgrade."

She also recommends specialising early. Jess shoots food and household products almost exclusively, which means her kitchen is already set up and a booking costs her half a day rather than two.

author: BookingModel Research
title: UGC vs. studio ads: a 2026 performance breakdown across 500 ad accounts
summary: Our analysis of 500+ brand ad accounts shows UGC outperforms studio-produced creative in 73 percent of A/B tests on Meta, with an average 1.8x CTR lift.
body:
We analysed anonymised performance data from more than 500 brand ad accounts running both creator-made and studio-produced creative during the first half of 2026. Every comparison below is drawn from tests where both creative types ran in the same account, in the same period, against the same audience.

## Headline findings

- UGC won 73 percent of head-to-head A/B tests on Meta
- Average CTR lift for the winning UGC variant: 1.8x
- Median cost per thousand impressions was 24 percent lower for UGC
- Studio creative won more often in one category: high-consideration purchases above $400

## Where UGC wins

The advantage is largest in the first three seconds. Creator-made openings — a face, a hand reaching for a product, an unedited voice — hold attention where a polished product shot does not. That gap compounds: more three-second views means more of the budget reaches people who actually watch.

Categories with the strongest UGC advantage were food and beverage, personal care, household goods and apparel under $80.

## Where studio creative still wins

Studio production kept its edge in furniture, electronics above $400, and anything where the buyer needs to see build quality clearly. In those categories the 73 percent figure inverts almost exactly.

The practical read is not "UGC always". It is that the cheaper format wins by default and the expensive format has to earn its place.

## Creative volume matters more than creative type

The strongest predictor of account performance in our sample was not which format a brand used. It was how many distinct creative concepts they tested per month. Accounts testing more than 12 concepts monthly outperformed accounts testing fewer than 4 by a wide margin, regardless of format.

UGC's real advantage may simply be that it makes that volume affordable.

## Method

Data covers 512 accounts, January to June 2026, all US-targeted, minimum $5,000 monthly spend. Comparisons use account-level matched pairs; accounts running only one creative type were excluded.
